## Summary

Opt-in 8th redaction layer that shells out to the user-installed [OpenAI Privacy Filter](https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter) (`opf`) binary. Runs only at condensation + export boundaries; per-turn writes stay on the existing 7-layer pipeline. Default-off; users opt in via `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled = true`.

**This PR was rewritten from `main` on 2026-05-14.** The first iteration accumulated review-fix scope across multiple bot review passes and reached ~3000 insertions. The rewrite keeps every real correctness/privacy fix found during that cycle while skipping speculative scope (~1547 insertions, 4 commits, 19 files). The original work is preserved at `feat/openai-privacy-filter-v1-backup` for reference.

## What's included

- Two public entry points (`StringWithPrivacyFilter`, `JSONLContentWithPrivacyFilter`) plus thin Bytes wrappers — four plain entry points unchanged so per-turn temp writes never invoke OPF
- `\x1e`-joined batched inference: one shell-out per scope amortizes the OPF cold-start across the whole transcript
- Process-scoped circuit breaker: first OPF failure disables it for the rest of the invocation (closes #1218)
- Split `createRedactedBlobFromFile` so per-turn temp writes (`addDirectoryToChanges`) stay on the plain pipeline while `copyMetadataDir` uses the OPF-enabled variant
- `PromptsRedactedContent` field on Write/UpdateCommittedOptions: pre-compute the joined-prompt redaction once in `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` and `condenseSingleCheckpoint` so multi-checkpoint commits don't re-run OPF N×
- Settings layer rejects unknown category names at parse time — silent zero-detection of a privacy category is effectively a correctness bug
- Sanitized stdout/stderr in shellout errors (OPF could echo input content; bytes-only diagnostics)
- `charToByteOffset` correct for multibyte UTF-8 (no off-by-one at end)
- `Span` docs reflect byte offsets (shellout adapter converts from OPF's character offsets)
- Inline shell-out runtime, label map, and progress UX in `redact/opf.go` — no `redact/opf_runtime/` subpackage, no separate progress writer

## What's intentionally NOT included (deferred to follow-ups)

- Summary-field batching via a `StringsWithPrivacyFilter` API — summaries are opt-in (only when `IsSummarizeEnabled`), have 5–10 short fields, and add ~10s worst case. Acceptable until someone complains.
- `doctor_bundle` per-entry batching — diagnostic command, runs rarely, worst case slow not broken.
- `on_failure` settings field — dropped entirely. `DisallowUnknownFields` rejects any user who tries to set it. Warn is the only supported mode today; if block-mode runtime wiring lands later, the field comes back in lockstep.

## Test plan

- [x] `mise run check` (fmt + lint + test:ci + Vogon canary + roger-roger external-agent canary) — all green on `672044c2f`
- [x] Real-agent smoke test on a fresh repo with `private_person` enabled — confirmed:
  - No `OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning transcript` during the agent turn (per-turn writes don't invoke OPF)
  - `→ scanning transcript… ✓ done (29.4s)` then `(2.3s)` at commit time (transcript + joined-prompts passes)
  - `[REDACTED_PERSON]` appears in `entire checkpoint explain HEAD` for both the prompt and the assistant transcript

392	// len(s) (the exclusive end position used as a slice bound).
393	func charToByteOffset(s string, charOff int) int {
394		if charOff < 0 {
395			return -1
396		}
397		byteOff := 0
398		for range charOff {
399			if byteOff >= len(s) {
400				return -1
401			}
402			_, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[byteOff:])
403			byteOff += size
404		}
405		return byteOff
406	}
407	
408	// partitionIndex returns the input index that contains [spanStart, spanEnd)
409	// within the concatenated batch, or -1 if the region crosses a separator
410	// boundary or is outside any input. starts[i] is the byte offset where
411	// inputs[i] begins; each input ends at starts[i+1] - len(sep), or at the
412	// end of the batched string for the last input.
413	func partitionIndex(starts []int, spanStart, spanEnd int, sep string) int {
414		if spanStart < 0 || spanEnd <= spanStart {
415			return -1
416		}
417		for i := range starts {
418			base := starts[i]
419			var end int
420			if i+1 < len(starts) {
421				end = starts[i+1] - len(sep)
422			} else {
423				// Last input — no upper bound tracked. Accept any span that
424				// starts >= base; the caller's bounds-check on the returned
425				// span's byte offsets covers the runaway case.
426				end = 1 << 31
427			}
428			if spanStart >= base && spanEnd <= end {
429				return i
430			}
431			if spanStart < base {
432				return -1
433			}
434		}
435		return -1
436	}

- **Batching pattern is elegant**: `\x1e` (ASCII Record Separator) as the join byte is a nice choice — it's whitespace-shaped for OPF's tokenizer (so spans don't get confused) yet won't collide with real content. The `partitionIndex` then maps batched-space offsets back to per-input offsets in O(n) — clean.
- **Process-scoped circuit breaker via atomic.Bool**: trips on first failure, resets on `ConfigurePrivacyFilter`. A `CompareAndSwap(false, true)` ensures only ONE user-facing warning even under concurrent first-call races.
- **Char→byte translation lives in the adapter, not callers**: `Span` documents byte offsets; OPF emits rune offsets; `charToByteOffset` does the conversion. This means callers can slice `[]byte` directly without re-walking UTF-8 — a small but important invariant.

781	-Entire automatically scans transcript and metadata content before writing it to the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. 784	 1. **Entropy scoring** — Identifies high-entropy strings (Shannon entropy > 4.5) that look like randomly generated secrets, even if they don't match a known pattern.

790	+### Optional OpenAI Privacy Filter (`opf`)
791	+
792	+A separate, **opt-in** layer that shells out to the [OpenAI Privacy Filter](https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter) (`opf`) — a 1.5B-parameter token-classification model that finds names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, dates, URLs, account numbers, and secrets that pure regex can miss. Disabled by default. Runs *in addition to* the seven built-in layers, only at the condensation and export boundaries (never per-turn), so the agent loop's hot path stays on the fast pipeline.
793	+
794	+Prerequisites:
795	+
796	+```bash
797	+pip install opf
798	+```
799	+
800	+Verify `opf --help` works; the CLI defaults to resolving the binary via `$PATH`. Override with the `command` setting if you need a specific path.
801	+
802	+Enable in `.entire/settings.json`:
803	+
804	+```json
805	+{
806	+  "redaction": {
807	+    "openai_privacy_filter": {
808	+      "enabled": true,
809	+      "categories": {
810	+        "private_person": true
811	+      }
812	+    }
813	+  }
814	+}
815	+```
816	+
817	+Available categories (set to `true` to enable, `false` or omit to skip):
818	+
819	+| Category | Replacement token | Notes |
820	+|---|---|---|
821	+| `private_person` | `[REDACTED_PERSON]` | Person names |
822	+| `private_email` | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` | Email addresses |
823	+| `private_phone` | `[REDACTED_PHONE]` | Phone numbers |
824	+| `private_address` | `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]` | Street addresses |
825	+| `private_url` | `[REDACTED_URL]` | URLs that may identify a person/account |
826	+| `private_date` | `[REDACTED_DATE]` | Dates (DOB, etc.) |
827	+| `account_number` | `[REDACTED_ACCOUNT_NUMBER]` | Account / card / SSN-shaped numbers |
828	+| `secret` | `REDACTED` | Generic credential-shaped values |
829	+
830	+Unknown category names are rejected at settings load time so typos surface immediately instead of silently disabling a category.
831	+
832	+Full settings reference:
833	+
834	+```json
835	+{
836	+  "redaction": {
837	+    "openai_privacy_filter": {
838	+      "enabled": true,
839	+      "categories": {
840	+        "private_person": true,
841	+        "private_email": true,
842	+        "private_phone": true,
843	+        "private_address": false,
844	+        "private_url": false,
845	+        "private_date": false,
846	+        "account_number": false,
847	+        "secret": false
848	+      },
849	+      "command": "opf",
850	+      "timeout_seconds": 30
851	+    }
852	+  }
853	+}
854	+```
855	+
856	+- `command` — path or PATH-resolvable name of the `opf` binary. Defaults to `opf`.
857	+- `timeout_seconds` — per-invocation timeout. Defaults to `30`.
858	+
859	+There is no `on_failure` setting; warn-on-failure is the only mode supported today. If OPF is not on PATH, fails to start, or times out, Entire prints a one-line `× OpenAI Privacy Filter unavailable …` notice and continues with the seven built-in layers. A per-process circuit breaker disables OPF for the remainder of the invocation after the first failure, so a broken install costs one warning rather than one timeout per redaction call.

861	+Cost note: each shell-out loads the OPF model (~1.5B parameters on CPU). Condensation batches all eligible leaf strings into a single inference pass per scope (transcript + joined prompts), so a typical real-world commit adds ~25–30s of OPF inference rather than the multi-minute cost a per-leaf flow would incur.

1027	+	for label, enabled := range cfg.Categories {

I have enough context. Here is my review.

---

## Review: PR #1214 — feat(redact): add OpenAI Privacy Filter as optional 8th detection layer

### Overview

Adds an opt-in 8th redaction layer that shells out to a user-installed `opf` binary (a ~1.5B-parameter token-classification model). The layer runs **only at condensation/export boundaries** — per-turn writes stay on the existing 7-layer pipeline — so the agent loop's hot path is unaffected. ~1.5K LOC across 19 files, dominated by `redact/opf.go` (436 LOC) and its test (481 LOC).

The interesting architectural decisions:
- **Split entry points**, not a runtime flag. Plain (`String`/`Bytes`/`JSONLBytes`) and OPF-augmented (`*WithPrivacyFilter`) functions are separate. The hot path can't accidentally invoke OPF — proved by the call graph, not enforced at runtime.
- **Batched inference via `\x1e`** (ASCII RS) join: one OPF shell-out per scope, not per leaf. Author claims ~25–30s per commit vs. multi-minute per-leaf cost.
- **Process-scoped circuit breaker** (`atomic.Bool`): first failure trips it for the rest of the invocation; one user-facing warning, not N timeouts.
- **`PromptsRedactedContent` short-circuit**: precompute the joined-prompts blob once in `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` so multi-checkpoint commits don't pay OPF N×.

### What's strong

- **Architectural cleanliness.** `createRedactedBlobFromFile` (plain, used by per-turn temp writes) vs `createRedactedBlobFromFileWithPrivacyFilter` (used by `copyMetadataDir` on the committed path). The split is enforced by call graph, with `TestPlainEntryPointsNeverInvokeOPF` as a regression guard. Clean and provable.
- **`charToByteOffset` + `partitionIndex`** correctly translate OPF's rune offsets to byte offsets and partition spans back to per-input. Edge cases (UTF-8 multibyte, end-of-string, span crossing separator) all have direct test coverage in `TestCharToByteOffset` / `TestPartitionIndex`.
- **Error hygiene.** `RedactBatch` deliberately omits stdout/stderr content from error strings (OPF could echo input fragments when misconfigured). Asserted by `TestShellOut_ExitError_DoesNotLeakStderr` and `TestShellOut_ParseError_DoesNotLeakStdout`. Good defense.
- **`WaitDelay: 500ms`** on `*exec.Cmd` ensures `cmd.Wait()` returns promptly when descendant processes hold pipes after a kill. Comment explains the Linux-CI motivation — non-obvious detail worth keeping.
- **`validateOPFSettings` rejects unknown category names at parse time.** Silent zero-detection of a privacy category would let a typo make a user think they're protected. `DisallowUnknownFields` + this check together also pin `on_failure` as nonexistent (tested explicitly).
- **`DisallowUnknownFields` round-trip** with category validation is covered on both the `LoadFromBytes` and merge paths. `TestLoadFromBytes_OPFSettings_Merge` exercises override semantics correctly.

### Issues worth addressing

**1. Test-only helpers are part of the public package API.**
`GetOPFConfigForTest` and `ResetOPFConfigForTest` are exported in `redact/opf.go`. Idiomatic Go puts these in an `export_test.go` (still `package redact`) so they're only visible to tests within the package. Today, any consumer of `github.com/entireio/cli/redact` can call them — risk is small but the API surface is wider than intended.

**2. Subtle behavioral change in `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` prompt redaction is not type-enforced.**
`manual_commit_hooks.go:2728-2756` — the old code mutated `prompts[i] = redact.String(p)` in place, then passed redacted prompts to `UpdateCommittedOptions.Prompts`. The new code leaves `prompts` UNREDACTED and supplies the redacted blob via `PromptsRedactedContent`. The writer (`committed.go:writeSessionToSubdirectory`) currently only uses `opts.Prompts` through `redactedJoinedPrompts(ctx, opts.Prompts, opts.PromptsRedactedContent)`, so it's safe today — but the invariant is enforced by inspection, not types. If a future change reads `opts.Prompts` for any other purpose (e.g., logging), raw prompts could leak. Worth either (a) a comment on the `Prompts` field warning that it may be unredacted when `PromptsRedactedContent` is set, or (b) a wrapper type like `RedactedBytes` to enforce this at compile time.

**3. `1 << 31` magic number in `partitionIndex`.**
`opf.go:432` — `end = 1 << 31` as a sentinel for "no upper bound" works but reads as a magic number. Prefer `math.MaxInt32` (or `math.MaxInt` if you don't care about width). One-line clarity fix.

**4. Progress-print code duplication.**
`detectOPF` and `JSONLContentWithPrivacyFilter`'s Pass 2 each print the same "scanning…" / "done (X.Xs)" pair to `opfStderr`. Small enough to live with, but a `withOPFProgress(opfStderr, func() error { ... })` helper would consolidate the two callsites and the timing measurement.

**5. `opfStderr = openTTYOrDiscard()` runs at package init.**
`opf.go:161` — opens `/dev/tty` once at process start, keeps the FD open for process lifetime. Two consequences:
- On systems where the user redirects stderr (`entire ... 2>log`), OPF progress messages still appear on the controlling TTY. This is intentional (documented in-comment) because the post-commit hook does `2>/dev/null`, but a user running `entire` in a fully scripted/captured context will see "ghost" output. Worth a brief mention in `docs/security-and-privacy.md`.
- The opened `*os.File` is never explicitly closed. Trivial leak (one FD, closes at exit), but tidier code would close on shutdown.

**6. `enabledCategories` returns `[]string` but `sort.Strings` is applied — comment says "deterministic order for tests + logs".**
Looks correct. Just noting: tests rely on this — if anyone changes the sort, expect `TestDetectOPF_*` to break.

**7. Coverage gap: no integration test asserting OPF's `"secret"` label produces bare `REDACTED`.**
The `opfLabelMap["secret"] = ""` mapping → `applyRegions` → `replacementToken("")` returns bare `REDACTED`. The single-string test `TestStringWithPrivacyFilter_AugmentsRegexLayers` covers PERSON. Worth adding a case that exercises the empty-label branch — it's a real product behavior (secrets render as `REDACTED`, not `[REDACTED_SECRET]`) and currently untested via the OPF path.

**8. `JSONLContentWithPrivacyFilter` happy-path assertion missing.**
`TestJSONLContentWithPrivacyFilter_BatchesSingleCall` asserts the batch count is 1; `TestJSONLContentWithPrivacyFilter_FallsBackOnBatchError` asserts non-empty output on fallback. No test checks that the returned content actually contains the redaction tokens for an OPF-tagged leaf. Easy to add and increases confidence that Pass 3's per-leaf "regex layers + cached OPF spans" path produces the right bytes.

**9. `\x1e` collision risk in inputs.**
The comment says U+001E "doesn't appear in real text." True for almost all transcripts, but not guaranteed for tool output or user prompts. If a leaf legitimately contains `\x1e`, the `partitionIndex` could miscount (a span starting before the embedded `\x1e` would still fit within its input's bounds, so usually fine; spans crossing it are dropped silently). Acceptable as v1 — but worth noting in a comment that this is a defensive-best-effort assumption.

### Correctness sanity-check

- **Byte/rune offset translation**: `RedactBatch` does `strings.ReplaceAll(in, "\n", " ")` before joining. Newlines and spaces are both 1 byte → byte offsets stay valid. Slicing the original `v` with these offsets in Pass 3 is safe. ✓
- **Bounds check in Pass 3**: `sp.End > len(v)` filters out OPF spans that exceed the input. Original-input length == flattened-input length (1-byte substitution), so the check is sound. ✓
- **Concurrent first failures**: `opfBreakerTripped.CompareAndSwap(false, true)` ensures only one of N concurrent first-failures prints the warning. ✓

### Performance

Both follow-ups are done. Summary of what changed:

**Item #1 — Test helpers moved to `export_test.go`** (`redact/`):
- Created `redact/export_test.go` containing `GetOPFConfigForTest` and `ResetOPFConfigForTest`. They keep the same names but are now invisible to importers — `redact` package no longer ships these in its public API. Internal `getOPFConfig` / `resetOPFConfig` stay in `opf.go`.

**Item #2 — Compile-time-enforced pre-redacted prompts**:
- New `redact.RedactedJoinedPrompts` type in `redact/redact.go` with a private `content string` field. Construct only via:
  - `redact.JoinedPrompts(ctx, prompts, sep) RedactedJoinedPrompts` — joins + runs the full 8-layer pipeline. Following the noun-named `String`/`Bytes`/`JSONLBytes` convention (revive flagged `RedactJoinedPrompts` for stutter).
  - `redact.AlreadyRedactedJoinedPrompts(s)` — trusted-source escape hatch, mirroring `redact.AlreadyRedacted`.
- `WriteCommittedOptions.PromptsRedactedContent string` → `PromptsRedacted redact.RedactedJoinedPrompts` (same on `UpdateCommittedOptions`). Field docstring on the raw `Prompts []string` now warns it's unredacted and must flow through `redactJoinedPrompts`.
- Two writer callsites in `strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go` and `manual_commit_hooks.go` now use `redact.JoinedPrompts(ctx, prompts, cpkg.PromptSeparator)`.
- Four reader callsites and the `checkpoint.redactedJoinedPrompts` helper updated to consume the typed value.
- Two prompt tests in `checkpoint/prompts_test.go` updated to use the new constructors.

**Verification**:
- `mise run fmt && mise run lint` — clean (zero issues)
- `mise run test` — all 5,359 tests pass except one pre-existing failure in `cmd/entire/cli/review` (`TestReviewSummaryTokenEnricher_LoadsCurrentSessionState`) that I confirmed fails on the unmodified PR head — unrelated to these changes
- `mise run test:integration` — 340/340 pass
- `mise run test:e2e:canary` — 4/4 pass

**Branch note**: changes are in `.worktrees/redact-v2` on local branch `feat/openai-privacy-filter-v2`. The PR (`#1214`) uses the remote branch `feat/openai-privacy-filter`. To land these, you'll want to either fast-forward `feat/openai-privacy-filter` to the new tip and push, or cherry-pick. Want me to prepare a commit on the right branch and push?

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The typed-wrapper pattern (`RedactedBytes`, now `RedactedJoinedPrompts`) is a lightweight version of Rust's "newtype" idiom — wrap a primitive in a one-field struct with a private field, and the type system enforces "you only got this by going through a sanctioned constructor." Costs zero runtime overhead since Go inlines single-field structs, and the constraint is checked at compile time rather than via assertions or tests.
- The revive stutter rule (`redact.Redact...`) nudged toward the cleaner `redact.JoinedPrompts(...) RedactedJoinedPrompts` naming, which matches the existing `redact.String(s) string` / `redact.Bytes(b) []byte` pattern. A good example of a lint hint pushing you toward an existing convention rather than fighting it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Context: we're shelling out to `opf` from a Go CLI, and the cold-start (loading the 1.5B-param token-classification model) dominates wall-clock time per invocation. We currently batch all eligible leaves from a transcript into ONE shell-out per condensation by joining with `\x1e` (single inference pass), which collapses N×cold-start to 1×cold-start. Even so, users see ~25–30s per real-world commit.

Investigate, in ~10 minutes:

1. Does the `opf` CLI support any kind of persistent / daemon / server mode? Look at the GitHub repo, README, CLI help, and any docs.
2. Does it support GPU / MPS (Apple Silicon) acceleration? We currently invoke with `--device cpu` — is there a faster default if a user has a GPU?
3. Is there a Python API that lets a user write their own daemon wrapper around the model object (i.e. load model once, serve multiple requests)?
4. Are there issues / discussions on the OpenAI repo about cold-start latency or daemon mode that suggest upstream is planning anything?
5. Any third-party patterns (community wrappers, FastAPI servers, etc.) that already solve this?

Report concise findings (~300 words max), structured as:
- Built-in OPF features that help (or don't)
- What we'd need to build on our end to amortize cold-start across commits — concretely, what would a daemon-mode implementation of the `opfRuntime` interface look like (Unix socket? stdio over a long-lived process? sidecar?)
- Recommendation for next step

Cite source URLs.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Moving OPF from post-commit to pre-push is the real performance win here, more than the prompt itself. Commits happen many times an hour; pushes maybe a few times. Same OPF cost, paid much less often.

Concretely, what this turns into:

**Architecture shift (the real work)**: today OPF runs at post-commit condensation, so the bytes on `entire/checkpoints/v1` are already OPF-redacted before push. Moving to pre-push means:
1. Post-commit writes checkpoints with the 7-layer pipeline only
2. Pre-push hook (`manual_commit_hooks.go` PrePush path) identifies unpushed `entire/checkpoints/v1` commits, runs OPF over their trees, rewrites them as new commits, pushes the new tip
3. Local branch fast-forwards to the rewritten tip

This is a non-trivial change to the pre-push flow but architecturally clean — checkpoint commit SHAs aren't referenced from anywhere else (user commits link by 12-hex `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer to tree paths, not SHAs), so rewriting is safe.

**Prompt layer (the UX)**: in the pre-push hook, before launching OPF:
- TTY: `huh` form with options `Yes / No / Always (this push)` — wired through `NewAccessibleForm`
- Non-interactive (no TTY): print `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning N checkpoints (may take 30s+)…` and proceed (matches your "if enabled, just print" preference)
- CLI flag: `entire push --opf=yes|no|always` to override the prompt non-interactively for scripts
- Settings: keep `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled` as-is; optionally add `prompt_default: "ask"|"always"|"never"` if you want a sticky default

Yes, that's the right mental model — with one nuance worth pinning down:

**Concretely what happens on `entire/checkpoints/v1`**:
- Post-commit: writes new commits with **7-layer-redacted blobs** (raw secrets gone, tagged tokens like `REDACTED`/`[REDACTED_EMAIL]` in place)
- Pre-push: reads those blobs, runs OPF over the already-redacted bytes, builds **new blobs with extended redaction** (adds `[REDACTED_PERSON]`, `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]`, etc.), creates new commits, fast-forwards the local branch, and pushes
- The 7-layer-only blobs/commits become unreachable locally (eventually GC'd) and **never reach the remote**

**The nuance**: because OPF sees the already-redacted text (not the raw original), it cannot double-tag content the 7 layers already caught. An email at `john@acme.com` becomes `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` after layer 7 — OPF then sees the bare token and doesn't re-redact it. That's fine in practice because OPF's main value is the *new* categories layer 7 doesn't catch (person names, street addresses, dates, account numbers). They're complementary, not redundant.

**One thing to be deliberate about**: if a user pushes once with OPF off, then turns it on and pushes again later, the *first* push already exfiltrated the 7-layer-only version. OPF's protection is forward-only from when it's enabled. Same caveat as today — but worth surfacing in docs/the prompt copy so users don't misjudge what they're protected from.

Yes, new commits on `entire/checkpoints/v1` — and to your second question: I think it actually is the best fit, *given* the constraints of this codebase. Let me explain why before defaulting to it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- `entire/checkpoints/v1` is CLI-owned infrastructure, not a user-facing branch. Nothing references its commit SHAs externally — the `Entire-Checkpoint: <12-hex>` trailer on the user's main-branch commits links by **tree path** (`<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/`), not by commit SHA. So rewriting those commits is invisible to every other part of the system, including the user's own commit history.
- Git's content-addressing model means there's no real distinction between "amending" and "creating a new commit" — any byte change produces a new SHA. The only question is whether you keep the old commit reachable somewhere (we shouldn't — it's a transient 7-layer-only stepping stone).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Why "rewrite at pre-push" wins over the alternatives:**

| Approach | What goes on remote | Local debuggability | Architectural cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rewrite commits at pre-push** (what I proposed) | 8-layer | Brief: 7-layer visible between commit and push | Low — pre-push hook already exists |
| Two parallel branches (`v1` local, `v1-redacted` remote) | 8-layer | Permanent: 7-layer stays local | Medium — doubles cleanup, status, explain logic |
| Side-car metadata (store OPF spans, apply at render time) | 7-layer bytes + spans JSON | Trivial | **Security regression** — raw bytes on remote aren't actually redacted |
| Async background OPF after commit | 8-layer eventually | Complex (in-flight state) | High — background processes, crash recovery, coordination |

Side-car (the third row) is the worst — it defeats the point of OPF as a redaction layer because anyone running `git cat-file blob` on the remote would see the unredacted-by-OPF text. The "redaction" only exists in our renderer, not in the bytes. Hard pass.

**The one design decision worth being deliberate about**: do we keep the 7-layer-only commits reachable somewhere after the rewrite, or do we let them become unreachable and GC'd?

- **GC'd (simpler, recommended)**: branch ref moves to the new 8-layer tip. Old commits become unreachable and disappear on the next `git gc`. No audit trail of "what OPF added."
- **Preserved as a debug ref** (e.g. `entire/checkpoints/v1-pre-opf/<sha>`): adds a refs namespace, useful for "show me what OPF caught" forensics, but adds cleanup logic and storage.

I'd go GC'd for v1. If users ever ask for "what did OPF actually redact in my last commit?" — that's a feature we can add later by keeping the old SHA briefly.

**One subtlety to handle correctly**: if a user pushes multiple times, each push only needs to rewrite checkpoints that haven't been OPF-processed yet. We can track this with a trailer on each `entire/checkpoints/v1` commit (`Entire-OPF-Applied: true`), so the second push doesn't re-redact what's already 8-layer.

Good catch — yes, briefly, locally, in three places. Worth understanding the actual mechanics:

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Git is **content-addressable and append-only at the object layer**. Moving a branch ref doesn't *delete* the old commit — it just makes it unreachable. The object stays in `.git/objects/` until `git gc --prune` sweeps it, which by default only runs after `gc.pruneExpire` (2 weeks).
- **Worktrees share `.git/objects/`** — so the old object is visible from any of your 73 worktrees, not just the one that did the rewrite.
- The reflog is the second hidden persistence layer: even if you never run `git cat-file -p OLD_SHA`, `git reflog show entire/checkpoints/v1` records every ref move with timestamps, keeping a paper trail for ~90 days (`gc.reflogExpire`).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Where the old 7-layer-only objects live after the rewrite:**

| Location | Persistence | Pushed to remote? |
|---|---|---|
| `.git/objects/` (unreachable loose/packed objects) | Until next `git gc --prune` (default: 2 weeks) | No — `git push` only sends reachable objects |
| `git reflog entire/checkpoints/v1` | Default 90 days, then expired | No — reflog is strictly local |
| Pack files (if already packed) | Same as loose objects, but `git gc` only repacks based on unreachable thresholds | No |

So nothing reaches the remote, but a local user can recover the 7-layer version for ~2 weeks via:
```
git cat-file -p $(git reflog show entire/checkpoints/v1 | awk 'NR==2 {print $1}')
```

**Does this matter?** Depends on your threat model:

- **"Don't leak PII to remote / shared infra"** — fine. The remote never sees it. This is the typical OPF use case.
- **"Don't leave PII recoverable anywhere, even locally"** — needs explicit cleanup. After the rewrite, run:

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

def test_specific_behavior():

```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")

- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.

```
func rewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF(ctx, repo, remoteName, opfDecision) (rewrittenTip plumbing.Hash, err error) {
    1. localRef = entire/checkpoints/v1 (return early if missing)
    2. remoteRef = <remoteName>/entire/checkpoints/v1 (may be ZeroHash if bootstrap)
    3. If !opfDecision.Run, return localRef as-is (push the 7-layer version verbatim)
    4. Compute unpushed set:
       unpushed = git.Log(From: localRef, ExcludeFrom: remoteRef)
       — equivalent to `git rev-list localRef ^remoteRef`; handles force-pushed remote correctly
       — bootstrap (remoteRef == ZeroHash): unpushed = entire reachable history of localRef
         (safety cap: if len > 100, abort with explicit error; user opts in via --force-bootstrap env)
    5. Order unpushed oldest-first.
    6. lastRewritten := remoteRef (the new parent chain's starting anchor)
    7. For each commit c in unpushed:
       if HasOPFApplied(c):
         // Already-applied: must still re-parent so the chain stays linear after rebuilds below it
         newCommit := rebuildCommit(c, parent=lastRewritten, tree=c.tree, preserveTrailers=true)
       else:
         newTree := rebuildTreeWithOPF(c.tree)  // see "Tree rewrite spec" below
         newCommit := buildCommit(
             tree=newTree,
             parent=lastRewritten,
             author/committer=c.author/c.committer,
             message=c.message + "\nEntire-OPF-Applied: true",
             preserveOtherTrailers=true,
         )
       lastRewritten = newCommit
    8. CAS ref: storer.CheckAndSetReference(
         new=NewHashReference(localRef, lastRewritten),
         old=NewHashReference(localRef, originalLocalTip),
       )
       — if CAS fails (concurrent push from another worktree), abort with retry guidance
    9. Return lastRewritten as the tip to push.
}
```

**Tree rewrite spec (`rebuildTreeWithOPF`):**

The v1 tree at `<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/` contains:
| Path | Action |
|---|---|
| `metadata.json` (checkpoint-level) | Copy verbatim (structural; no user text) |
| `<i>/metadata.json` (per-session) | Copy verbatim |
| `<i>/full.jsonl` | OPF via `redact.JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` on the 7-layer-redacted content |
| `<i>/prompt.txt` | OPF via `redact.BytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `<i>/content_hash.txt` | **Recompute** as SHA256 of the new `full.jsonl` bytes |
| `<i>/tasks/<tool-use-id>/agent-*.jsonl` | OPF via `redact.JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `<i>/tasks/<tool-use-id>/checkpoint.json` | Copy verbatim (UUID mapping; no user text) |

**Contract**: OPF runs over already-7-layer-redacted bytes. The OPF detector sees regex tokens like `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` as opaque text; it adds only the categories the regex layers miss (PERSON, ADDRESS, etc.). This contract is enforced by a unit test: feed OPF a fixture containing `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` and assert it isn't re-tagged.

**Required tests:**
- Happy path: unpushed includes 3 unapplied commits → all 3 rewritten in order, ref CAS'd
- Mixed history: unpushed = [applied, unapplied, applied] → all 3 re-parented in chain; only middle one's tree changes
- Force-pushed remote: remote ref points to unrelated commit → unpushed via `^remote` excludes the divergent base; only local-only commits are rewritten
- Bootstrap: remote ref missing, unpushed = 50 commits → succeeds; unpushed = 101 commits → errors with bootstrap guidance
- OPF runtime failure mid-rewrite: circuit breaker trips, function aborts with no ref change (no half-written state)
- CAS conflict: simulate ref change after read → returns error with "another push in progress" wording
- Tree contract: rebuild a tree, assert `content_hash.txt` matches SHA256 of new `full.jsonl`
- Tree-path preservation: rebuilt tree still has `<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/` layout; `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer in user commit can still resolve metadata via path

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Git worktrees create isolated workspaces sharing the same repository, allowing work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching.

**Core principle:** Systematic directory selection + safety verification = reliable isolation.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace."

## Directory Selection Process

Follow this priority order:

### 1. Check Existing Directories

```bash
# Check in priority order
ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
```

**If found:** Use that directory. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

### 2. Check CLAUDE.md

```bash
grep -i "worktree.*director" CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null
```

**If preference specified:** Use it without asking.

### 3. Ask User

If no directory exists and no CLAUDE.md preference:

```
No worktree directory found. Where should I create worktrees?

1. .worktrees/ (project-local, hidden)
2. ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/<project-name>/ (global location)

Which would you prefer?
```

## Safety Verification

### For Project-Local Directories (.worktrees or worktrees)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
# Check if directory is ignored (respects local, global, and system gitignore)
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:**

Per Jesse's rule "Fix broken things immediately":
1. Add appropriate line to .gitignore
2. Commit the change
3. Proceed with worktree creation

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

### For Global Directory (~/.config/superpowers/worktrees)

No .gitignore verification needed - outside project entirely.

## Creation Steps

### 1. Detect Project Name

```bash
project=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")
```

### 2. Create Worktree

```bash
# Determine full path
case $LOCATION in
  .worktrees|worktrees)
    path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
  ~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/*)
    path="~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/$project/$BRANCH_NAME"
    ;;
esac

# Create worktree with new branch
git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

### 3. Run Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

### 4. Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure worktree starts clean:

```bash
# Examples - use project-appropriate command
npm test
cargo test
pytest
go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### 5. Report Location

```
Worktree ready at <full-path>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Neither exists | Check CLAUDE.md → Ask user |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Mistakes

### Skipping ignore verification

- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status
- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree

### Assuming directory location

- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions
- **Fix:** Follow priority: existing > CLAUDE.md > ask

### Proceeding with failing tests

- **Problem:** Can't distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues
- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed

### Hardcoding setup commands

- **Problem:** Breaks on projects using different tools
- **Fix:** Auto-detect from project files (package.json, etc.)
